Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, the November ballot includes nine citizens’ initiatives. Most likely voters agree with the statement that there are too many propositions on the state ballot (37% strongly agree, 40% somewhat). Most across demographic, partisan, and regional groups agree at least somewhat. Three in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups strongly agree with this view, with the exception of 18- to 34-year-olds (16% strongly).
Majorities of likely voters say they would vote yes (58%, 40% no) on Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent. Support for Proposition 3 varies across partisan groups. Proposition 3 garners majority support among most demographic and regional groups, but opinions are more divided among likely voters who are white (48% support), age 55 and older (46%), and reside in the Central Valley (48%).
Six in ten likely voters (61%) would vote yes on Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers); about one in three would vote no (35%). If passed, it would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages of newly constructed homes below $1.5 million. Solid majorities of Democrats (76%) and independents (62%) would vote yes, compared to fewer Republicans (35%). Majorities across demographic and regional groups would vote yes.
Majorities of likely voters (55%, 42% no) support Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half or more across demographic and regional groups support Proposition 38, with exceptions among likely voters who are white (46%) and those in the Central Valley (44%).
Four in ten likely voters (43%, 55% no) say they would vote yes on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification), which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Over eight in ten Republicans (85%) are in support, compared to far fewer independents (43%) and Democrats (19%). Support falls short at half or below among most demographic and regional groups, with exceptions among those age 55 and older and residents in the Central Valley and Inland Empire (57% each).
After reading the ballot title and label, 52 percent of California likely voters say they would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; 46 percent would vote no. About seven in ten Democrats (72%) would vote yes on this citizens’ initiative, compared to nearly half of independents (46%) and just two in ten Republicans (21%). The share of likely voters in support varies across demographic and regional groups, and support for Proposition 40 declines sharply as age increases.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 44% no) on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Three in four Republicans and half of independents (51%) support this proposition, compared to about four in ten Democrats (38%). Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
When it comes to Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate, a majority of likely voters would vote yes (54%, 43% no). Partisan views vary, with three in four Republicans (74%) and six in ten independents (61%) saying they would vote yes, compared to four in ten Democrats (39%). Half or more across most demographic and regional groups are in support, but this share falls short of half among likely voters in the San Francisco Bay Area (45%), those earning under $40,000 (43%), renters (41%), and those age 18 to 34 (36%).
Just one in three likely voters in the state say they would vote yes (34%, 61% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. Roughly one in three across partisan groups would vote yes, and about four in ten or fewer across demographic and regional groups are in support.
When it comes to Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review)— which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals— likely voters are divided (49% yes, 46% no). Roughly half or fewer among partisans would vote yes if the election were held today. Views vary across demographic and regional groups, with likely voters who are Latino (55%) and those earning $40,000 to $99,999 (56%) among the most likely to express support.
State of the State
Majorities of California adults (54%) and likely voters (52%) say the state is headed in the wrong direction. This belief is held by nearly all Republicans (94%) and a majority of independents (55%), compared to one in three Democrats (32%). Residents in the Central Valley (62%), the Inland Empire (62%), and Orange/San Diego (56%) are more pessimistic about the direction of the state than those in Los Angeles (48%) and the San Francisco Bay Area (46%).
Californians are much more pessimistic about economic conditions over the next year, with seven in ten adults (71%) and likely voters (73%) as well six in ten or more across parties (61% Democrats, 90% Republicans, 72% independents) expecting bad economic times for the state. About seven in ten Californians have been pessimistic about the economy since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/), and majorities have held this view since November 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-economic-well-being-november-2021/). Today, economic pessimism is widespread, with two in three or more across regions and demographic groups expecting bad economic times in the next year.
When asked if California is divided into two economic groups, the haves and have-nots, seven in ten adults (70%) and likely voters (69%) say the state is divided this way. When asked which economic group they are in, 55 percent of adults and 63 percent of likely voters say they are part of the haves.
About six in ten Californians and half of likely voters say recent price increases have caused financial hardship for them and their household. Findings were similar in May and over half of Californians have said price increases have caused hardship each time we’ve asked this question dating back to March 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-march-2022/). Today, majorities of Democrats (55%), independents (55%), and Republicans (51%) say recent price increases have caused hardship, as do majorities across regions. Hardship declines sharply across income groups, and there are notable differences across racial/ethnic groups, with Latinos (68%) and African Americans (64%) more likely than Asian Americans (46%) and whites (52%) to say recent price increases have caused hardship.
In addition to rising prices, many Californians say the cost of housing places a financial strain on their family, with 24 percent saying a lot of strain and 20 percent saying a little strain. Views were nearly identical last December (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-december-2025/) (25% a lot, 20% a little). The share saying housing costs place financial strain on their family decreases sharply with rising income (67% less than $40,000, 57% $40,000 to $99,999, 32% $100,000 or more). Majorities of African Americans (54%) and Latinos (52%) say housing costs place a strain on their finances, compared to fewer than four in ten Asian Americans (37%) and whites (36%).
Half of adults and likely voters continue to approve of the way Gavin Newsom is handling his job as governor. Approval is shaped by partisan views with most Democrats approving, while independents are divided, and nearly all Republicans disapprove. Residents in Los Angeles and the San Francisco Bay Area are more approving than those elsewhere. Majorities of African Americans, Latinos, and Asian Americans approve, while fewer whites do so.
Views of the California State Legislature are somewhat similar. Forty-five percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the job the state legislature is doing. Partisans disagree on legislative approval with two in three Democrats approving, while nine in ten Republicans and half of independents disapprove. Across regions and demographic groups, approval is highest among San Francisco Bay Area residents (55%), college graduates (53%), Asian Americans (52%), and Latinos (51%).
When asked about trust in government, four in ten Californians say they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right just about always (4%) or most of the time (36%), while six in ten say state government can be trusted only some of the time (59%). Views are nearly identical when asked about trust in local government (4% just about always, 37% most of the time, 58% only some of the time).
State of the Nation
Just two months before the consequential 2026 midterm elections, about eight in ten Californians (79% adults, 77% likely voters) think things in the nation are generally going in the wrong direction. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (80%) share this view, while about half of Republicans (52%) think the nation is going in the right direction. Overwhelming majorities across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians overall are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (69%), according to an August Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-08/Reuters%20Ipsos%20August%20Core%20Political%20Topline.pdf) poll. Overwhelming majorities of Californians also expect bad economic times for the country over the next year (76% adults, 75% likely voters).
Meanwhile, about a quarter approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (23% adults, 27% likely voters). Even fewer approve of the way Congress is handling its job (17% adults, 16% likely voters). This is a record low approval rating of Donald Trump across both his terms. Overwhelming majorities of Democrats (94%) and independents (78%) disapprove of Donald Trump; two in three Republicans (66%) approve—a significant decline from 84 percent in February 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2025/). Two in three or more Californians across demographic groups and regions disapprove of the president and Congress.
When asked about their level of trust in the federal government in Washington, eight in ten California adults (80%) and likely voters (83%) say they can trust it to do what is right only some of the time. In comparison, far fewer trust the federal government just about always (2% adults, 2% likely voters) or most of the time (16% adults, 13% likely voters). The overall share saying they trust the federal government only some of the time was similar last June (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/) (79%). Today, two in three or more across partisan groups, regions, and demographic groups say they trust the federal government to do what is right only some of the time.
Seven in ten Californians say they are very (41% adults, 46% likely voters) or somewhat (29% adults, 26% likely voters) dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care in the country. Overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents are dissatisfied, including more than half of Democrats (55%) who say they are very dissatisfied. A majority of Republicans say they are satisfied (10% very, 46% somewhat). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups say they are dissatisfied.
Seven in ten adults and two in three likely voters also believe that the federal government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care, while about three in ten believe health care access is an individual’s own responsibility. Nine in ten Democrats and seven in ten independents say ensuring access to health care is the federal government’s responsibility, while seven in ten Republicans say it is an individual’s responsibility to secure their own access to health care. Residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles are more likely than residents elsewhere in the state to say the federal government has this responsibility. Seven in ten or more African Americans (85%), Latinos (75%), and Asian Americans (71%) say ensuring access to health care is the federal government’s responsibility, compared to a smaller majority of white adults (57%). The share who views this as the federal government’s responsibility declines with rising age and income.
Four in ten Californians say the Democratic Party has a lot (11%) or some (29%) good ideas, while an additional three in ten (28%) say it has a few good ideas. About a quarter (23%) say it has almost no good ideas, and one in ten are unsure (9%). About two in three Democrats say their party has a lot or some good ideas, while two in three Republicans (66%) say the Democratic Party has almost no good ideas. African Americans and Latinos are more likely than Asian Americans and whites to say the Democratic Party has at least some good ideas.
About a quarter of California adults say the Republican Party has a lot (9%) or some (17%) good ideas, while an additional two in ten (22%) say it has a few good ideas. More than four in ten say it has almost no good ideas (44%), and one in ten are unsure (10%). Seven in ten Republicans say their party has at least some good ideas. Seven in ten Democrats and four in ten independents say the Republican Party has almost no good ideas. Across regions, residents in the Central Valley are the most likely to say the Republican Party has at least some good ideas. A majority of San Francisco Bay Area (53%) residents and nearly half of Los Angeles (48%) residents say it has almost no good ideas.
When asked about politicians who identify as democratic socialists, about three in ten Californians say they have a lot (12%) or some (19%) good ideas, while two in ten say they have a few good ideas (20%) and three in ten (31%) say they have almost no good ideas. However, nearly two in ten (17%) are unsure. Notably, a majority of Democrats say these politicians have at least some good ideas, compared to three in ten independent and 5 percent of Republicans. Seven in ten Republicans say these politicians have almost no good ideas.
San Francisco Bay Area residents are the most likely to say democratic socialist politicians have at least some good ideas while Inland Empire residents are the least likely to say so. Young adults age 18 to 34 (38%) are more likely than adults 55 and over (28%) to think these politicians have good ideas. College graduates (38%) are more likely than residents who have no college experience (25%) to say this (33% some college). According to a July Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-07/Reuters%20Ipsos%20July%20Core%20Political%20Topline%207.27.26_0.pdf) poll, Californians’ views of the ideas of the Democratic Party and Democratic socialist politicians are similar to the views of Americans overall, while Californians’ views of the Republican Party’s ideas are much more negative.

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner, survey analyst Lauren Mora; and survey analyst Deja Thomas, who was the project manager for this survey. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,745 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14.2 minutes. The survey was conducted from September 4–10, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West wants voters to change how community health clinics spend money and penalize those that violate the ballot initiative’s provisions.

Prop.
44 would require community health clinics, known as federally qualified health centers, to spend 90% of their revenue on “program services” that advance their mission to provide charitable care to low-income and uninsured patients.
The proposition would prohibit clinics from spending more than 10% of revenue on other things such as administrative expenses.
It would also penalize clinics that don’t meet the new 90% spending threshold.
The attorney general could fine clinics that don’t comply, and the money would go into a special fund reserved for health workforce spending.
Community health clinics are nonprofits that are required by law to reinvest 100% of revenue back into the organization regardless of how voters decide on Prop.
44.
Most clinics spend about 80% of revenue providing health services, although some spend less, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.

California's community health clinics are facing a 90% spending rule under Proposition 44, which would penalize nonprofit clinics that spend less on patient services.
Proposition 44 would require California's nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue each year on patient services and the work that supports them, or pay the difference to the state as a penalty.
The clinics it covers are Federally Qualified Health Centers: the network of safety-net clinics that provide primary, dental and mental health care to low-income and uninsured patients, many of them on Medi-Cal.
Prop 44 is an initiative statute placed on the ballot by petition, and its sponsor and sole funder is SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, a health care workers union.
It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide, and it trails by 27 points in the only poll that has tested it: 34% yes and 61% no in PPIC's September survey, with nearly identical margins among Democrats, Republicans and independents.

PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Safety Net Clinics Serve Low-Income People. Clinics are places where people can access certain health care services, such as doctor’s visits. Many clinics are considered “safety net,” as they mainly serve low-income and uninsured people. The care they provide is often low cost or free to patients. There are about 2,000 safety net clinics in California. Most are private nonprofits, and the rest are run by public entities (such as counties).
Clinics Spend Most of Their Revenue on Health Care Services. Clinics spend most of their revenue on providing health care to patients. They also have other expenses, such as administrative costs. Each year, private nonprofit safety net clinics in California report their revenues and expenses to the federal government and the state. These clinics currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of their revenue on providing health care services, though the percent varies across clinics.
PROPOSAL
Sets Minimum Spending on Health Care at Private Nonprofit Safety Net Clinics. Proposition 44 requires private nonprofit safety net clinics to spend at least 90 percent of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. This means that spending on other expenses, such as administrative costs, would be limited to no more than 10 percent of revenue. The California Attorney General would define in more detail which kinds of expenses are related to providing health care services, and which are other expenses, using existing reports to the federal government as a starting point. Affected clinics could ask the state for a temporary waiver of the requirements in some cases.
Creates Penalty for Falling Short of Minimum. Proposition 44 requires affected clinics to pay a penalty to the state if they fall short of the new health care spending minimum. The penalty would equal the amount of spending needed to reach the 90 percent minimum. Clinics could get their money back if they comply with the spending requirements within five years. If clinics do not comply within five years, the state would keep the money and spend it on clinic workforce programs.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Creates State Enforcement Costs. Under Proposition 44, the state would enforce the new requirements on private nonprofit safety net clinics. This includes reviewing financial reports and investigating affected entities. State enforcement costs would be in the low tens of millions of dollars per year. The proposition directs the state to cover the costs by charging fees on affected clinics.
Could Have Other Uncertain Costs. Proposition 44 could create other costs for the state and local governments. These costs are uncertain. They depend on (1) how the state Attorney General would define health care-related expenses and (2) whether affected clinics would meet the spending minimum. For example, affected clinics might spend more on direct health care services to comply with the requirement, which could increase state costs. This is because some of these services would be for patients in Medi-Cal, the state’s program that provides health care coverage for low-income Californians. Some clinics that could not meet the minimum spending requirement might close instead. This would create other uncertain effects on state and local costs.

REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 44
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST AND HOLD CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE.
California’s community health clinics receive billions of taxpayer dollars to provide care for people who need it most. Yet some clinics spend less than half of their funding on patient care and services, while large portions of their revenue go to bloated CEO salaries and other wasteful spending. As a result, patients wait months for appointments and healthcare workers struggle with staffing shortages, outdated equipment, and limited resources.
WHY PROP. 44 IS NEEDED
Community health clinics receive taxpayer funding for one purpose: to provide primary care, mental health services, dental care, prenatal care, vaccinations, and other essential services to millions of children, seniors, working families, and Californians with disabilities. Without access to these clinics, many patients would not get the care they urgently need. But some clinic CEOs are misusing taxpayer dollars by diverting millions to inflated executive salaries and other non-essentials.
With massive federal healthcare cuts expected to eliminate billions in funding for California’s healthcare system, community clinics will be among the hardest hit. Clinics may be forced to reduce services, lay off staff, or even close their doors. That means every healthcare dollar matters more than ever. California taxpayers can’t afford to waste resources that should be helping patients receive timely, high-quality care.
PROP. 44 DIRECTS HEALTHCARE DOLLARS TO PATIENT CARE
Proposition 44 is simple. It requires community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on their non-profit mission-patient care and the services that make care possible. That could include medical visits, mental health care, dental care, medications, medical equipment, transportation, language interpretation, care coordination, outreach, and other services that serve the clinics’ charitable healthcare mission.
What doesn’t count towards the 90%: excessive CEO pay, lavish events, bloated overhead, and other spending that takes resources away from the clinic’s core mission of caring for patients.
PROP. 44 HOLDS CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE
Proposition 44 will increase transparency by requiring clinics to publicly report how healthcare dollars are spent, so patients and taxpayers can hold them accountable. Currently, there are hundreds of millions of dollars in the clinic system that are not being spent on the core mission of patient care. Prop. 44 will make sure those healthcare dollars go where they can do the most good.
This measure does not cut clinic funding or reduce services patients rely on. Clinics that meet the standard keep every dollar, and even clinics that fall short can recover any penalties by coming into compliance. Unrecovered penalties, if any, are redirected to recruiting, training, and retaining the healthcare workers our clinics desperately need. Every dollar stays in the healthcare system-prioritized for patient care instead of excessive overhead.
Join healthcare workers, patients, and Californians who believe accountability strengthens our healthcare system.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST.
Shawna Brown , Initiative Proponent
Brisa J. Barrera , Community Clinic Worker
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 44
PROP. 44 IS A DANGEROUS SPECIAL INTEREST MEASURE THAT THREATENS CARE FOR MILLIONS
Make no mistake: Prop. 44 is not about resources for patient care. Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure written and funded entirely by one special interest that threatens access to care for millions. Prop. 44 imposes unworkable restrictions that actually prevent community clinics from providing the care patients need.
NURSES, DOCTORS AND PATIENT ADVOCATES ALL AGREE: PROP. 44 WILL HURT PATIENTS. Prop. 44 will:
• Cut billions from health clinics every year. • Force clinics to shut down and cut services. • Eliminate care for millions. • Send more patients to hospital ERs-increasing wait times for all families.
PROP. 44 IS UNNECESSARY. COMMUNITY CLINICS ARE STRICTLY REGULATED.
Community clinics are heavily regulated, with strict rules requiring resources be spent on patient care and serving their communities. Federal and state laws require regular audits and public reporting of clinic spending. Every community clinic is not-for-profit-led by a board that includes patients-requiring funds to be spent on patient care and community benefits-not corporate profits.
SPECIAL INTERESTS PUSHING PROP. 44 ARE USING PATIENTS AS PAWNS
Prop. 44 is a shameful power play by one special interest abusing the ballot measure process to gain political leverage over health clinics. This same special interest has spent $140 million pushing dozens of harmful ballot measures against hospitals, clinics and physicians, including three unsuccessful dialysis propositions that voters overwhelmingly rejected.
JOIN PATIENTS, NURSES, DOCTORS, AND COMMUNITY LEADERS: NO ON PROP. 44.
Prop. 44 is opposed by:
• American Academy of Pediatrics CA • California School Nurses Organization • California Medical Association • American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists District IX • Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA • American College of Emergency Physicians CA • California Academy of Family Physicians
www.NoProp44.com
Brent K Sugimoto , MD, FAAFP, President-Elect
California Academy of Family Physicians
Kelly McCue , MD, Immediate Past Chair
American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists District IX
Susanne J. Spano , MD, FACEP, President
American College of Emergency Physicians, California Chapter
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 44
VOTE NO ON PROP. 44: STOP THE ATTACK ON PATIENTS & COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS
Prop. 44 is a dangerous, poorly drafted measure that would threaten care for millions of California patients.
Prop. 44 imposes deeply flawed and unworkable restrictions that prevent community clinics from providing the care patients need. Economic and health experts warn Prop. 44 will:
• Cut $1.7 billion from health clinics in the first year alone. • Cause 88% of all clinics in the state to operate at a loss. • Force thousands of clinics throughout the state to cut back patient services or shut down entirely. • Eliminate care for millions of Californians. • Send more patients to hospital emergency rooms-increasing wait times for all families.
PROP. 44 ARBITRARILY RESTRICTS SPENDING ON VITAL PATIENT SERVICES
Prop. 44 is so poorly written that it restricts clinics from spending resources on essential staff and services, including nurse managers, physician leaders, translation services, insurance assistance and community education. It even restricts clinics from funding mammogram, X-ray and CT machines, information technology and expanding or upgrading clinics.
PROP. 44 DECIMATES THE HEALTH CARE SYSTEM AND HURTS ALL PATIENTS
Community health clinics provide primary care, prenatal care, urgent care, mental and behavioral health services, telehealth, and dental services. They operate school-based health clinics that care for hundreds of thousands of children.
Community clinics serve 1 in 4 Medi-Cal patients, the uninsured, working families, seniors, veterans, and children. In many rural and medically underserved communities, community health clinics are the only source of care within hundreds of miles.
Prop. 44 will make our bad healthcare problems even worse- increasing patient wait times and eliminating the only source of care for many patients.
PROP. 44 IS UNNECESSARY. COMMUNITY CLINICS ARE STRICTLY REGULATED.
Community clinics are already heavily regulated by the federal and state governments, with strict funding rules on patient care and essential services, and regular mandatory public audits. All clinics are overseen by patient board members, to ensure care is focused on community needs. And clinics are non-profits legally required to focus resources on patient services and community benefits.
PROP. 44 OPPOSED BY PATIENTS, NURSES, DOCTORS AND COMMUNITY LEADERS
“Prop. 44 will eliminate the only source of care in many communities. Please vote NO.” -Kim Yu, MD, FAAFP, President, California Academy of Family Physicians
“Community clinics are a lifeline for my family and millions across California. Please, protect patients like me. Reject Prop. 44.” -Carmen Huertero, Clinic Patient, San Marcos, CA
“Prop. 44 threatens women’s access to healthcare at a time when it’s already under attack. Vote No.” -Jodi Hicks, President & CEO, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California
"By shutting down clinics, Prop. 44 will force millions of patients into already overcrowded emergency rooms-increasing wait times for everyone.” -Susanne J Spano, MD, FACEP, President, American College of Emergency Physicians, California
“Prop. 44 threatens to shut down hundreds of school-based clinics that provide primary care, vaccinations, health screenings and mental health services for tens of thousands of children. Vote NO.” -Katie Nilsson, RN, President, California School Nurses Organization
Prop. 44 Opposed By:
• American Academy of Pediatrics, California • California School Nurses Organization • California Medical Association • California Primary Care Association, representing thousands of community health centers and clinics • American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists District IX • Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California • National Association of Social Workers, California Chapter • American College of Emergency Physicians, California • California Academy of Family Physicians
www.NoProp44.com
Eric Ball , MD, FAAP, President
American Academy of Pediatrics, California
Katie Nilsson , RN, President
California School Nurses Organization
René Bravo , M.D., President
California Medical Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 44
DON’T BE FOOLED BY SCARE TACTICS.
Highly paid clinic executives want you to believe this measure will close clinics, eliminate services, and hurt patients. Those claims are false.
PROP. 44 PROTECTS PATIENT CARE-IT DOESN'T CUT IT.
Proposition 44 simply requires that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ non-profit mission: patient care and services that support care. This CAN INCLUDE: Transportation, language interpretation, care coordination, community outreach, nurse managers and clinical staff, medical equipment and information technology, and mental health, dental, and preventative care. The opposition falsely claims these services would be cut, but Prop. 44 is designed to protect spending that serves patients.
PROP. 44 PREVENTS PRECIOUS RESOURCES FROM BEING DIVERTED AWAY FROM PATIENT CARE
Prop. 44 seeks to reduce spending on: Excessive CEO pay, lavish events, expensive consultants, and unnecessary administrative spending. That means healthcare dollars would go where they belong: Caring for patients.
WHY ARE CLINIC EXECUTIVES FIGHTING ACCOUNTABILITY?
The campaign against Prop. 44 is funded by the same highly paid clinic executives who benefit from the current system. If today’s oversight were enough, some clinics wouldn’t be spending less than half of their funding on patient care and services. The real threat to clinics isn’t accountability, it’s devastating federal healthcare cuts. Patients can’t afford to see precious funding spent on excessive CEO compensation and other non-essentials while they wait months for appointments and healthcare workers struggle with understaffing and limited resources.
PUT PATIENTS FIRST, NOT CLINIC CEOS.
Vote YES on Proposition 44.
Shawna Brown , Initiative Proponent
Brisa J. Barrera , Community Clinic Worker

A forgotten ballot measure? Union behind billionaire tax spends little on Prop. 44
By Ben Paviour
October 19, 2026 5:00 AM
Critics of Proposition 44 hold signs at a meeting of the resolutions committee of the California Democratic Party’s Executive Committee on Aug. 1, 2026. The measure would place new restrictions on how California’s federally-funded healthcare clinics spend money.
Ben Paviour
ben.paviour@sacbee.com
The union that put the billionaire tax on the ballot has put little money behind its other measure, Proposition 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317016992.html), a low-polling measure focused on health clinic spending.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West spent a little more than $20,000 on Prop. 44 from July 1 to Sept. 19, according to its most recent campaign filings, while opponents spent more than $32 million in the same period.
The SEIU-UHW appears to have concentrated its limited resources onProp. 40, a nationally-watched effort (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html) to impose a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth to offset federal healthcare cuts. The “Yes on 40” campaign spent $4.4 million during the period — still less than 10% of the total spent by billionaire tax opponents.
A Public Policy Institute of California poll released in mid-September (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) found Prop. 44 was the least popular propositions surveyed, with 34% of likely voters saying they supported the measure. Prop. 40, on the other hand, showed 52% support, though subsequent surveys have showed lower levels of support.
Prop. 44 would require federally-funded health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on patient services, a move SEIU-UHW says would strengthen accountability. Critics like the California Primary Care Association argue the measure is poorly designed and was sponsored by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan to win concessions from clinics SEIU-UHW is seeking to unionize.
Last month, the CPCA and five clinics filed a lawsuit accusing Regan and his union of racketeering. They argued he launches “punitive, harmful, and often long-shot and repetitive statewide or local ballot initiatives that are used as bargaining chips to extort broad concessions.” The case has yet to be heard.
The CPCA filed a lawsuit in April seeking to keep Prop. 44 off the ballot. A federal judge dismissed the case in August, saying the plaintiffs lacked standing.
Loading…
SEIU-UHW spokesperson Renée Saldaña said the union had not abandoned Prop. 44 and denied that bringing it was a negotiating tactic, calling the allegations in the latest lawsuit “categorically false.”
“Our path to victory is making sure voters understand what Prop 44 does: with federal cuts putting enormous pressure on California’s healthcare system, it ensures clinics that receive public funding spend that money on patient care,” Saldaña said. “SEIU-UHW members will be making that case through Election Day.”
No on 44 spokesperson Molly Weedn said they remained committed to defeating the measure.
“It’s shameful that UHW would put such a dangerous measure on the ballot and force community clinics to mount a campaign to defeat it, especially when there is so much work to do in communities ensuring people are getting the healthcare they need and deserve,” Weedn said in an email.

DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.

ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman

Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.
LOS ANGELES
Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks during a campaign event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Sylmar, California. | William Liang/AP
POWER PLAY — Frustration over sky-high electricity bills is becoming a flashpoint in the closing days of the Los Angeles mayor’s race, with Karen Bass and her progressive challenger, Nithya Raman , trading blows over utility costs that have soared amid record-breaking heatwaves, Alex Nieves reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/the-la-mayors-race-goes-electric-01137758).
The fracas began early last week after Raman held a press conference alongside frustrated Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers, where the council member blamed Bass for letting the utility raise electricity and water rates without City Council approval — and promised to audit the department. Bass has responded with promises to lower bills and investigate the city’s climbing utility costs.
The last-minute brawl comes as candidates statewide contend with high electricity prices and broader concerns about the cost of living — an issue (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) which is among voters’ top concerns. California’s electricity rates are the second-highest in the U.S., behind only Hawaii. Read last night’s California Currents (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-currents/2026/10/27/ramans-electric-closing-message-01137445) to see how both campaigns are trying to navigate energy affordability angst ahead of Election Day.
Top Talkers
UCLA SUIT — For the second time this month, the University of California has asked a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit by the Department of Justice alleging that UCLA failed to properly address antisemitic incidents during protests over Israel’s war against Hamas.
In a motion filed later Monday, UC officials acknowledged that “there is no question that some University employees were exposed to antisemitism on campus” but called the Trump administration’s claims of a campus overrun by it “flawed,” Eric He reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/uc-seeks-to-dismiss-another-doj-antisemitism-lawsuit-01136943).

Here’s what to know about Prop. 44 by Kristen Hwang (https://calmatters.org/author/kristen-hwang/) October 7, 2026 October 6, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) Dr. Navdeep Lehga sets up equipment in the exam room of the Saint Agnes Mobile Health Unit mobile clinic parked in the parking lot of Rojas Pierce Park in Mendota on Aug. 28, 2025. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local IN SUMMARY Proposition 44 would require clinics to spend more money on patient care. The union pushing the measure is the same one supporting the billionaire tax proposal. Clinics say the measure will force closures. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. The same union that put forward the billionaire wealth tax has another, lesser-known proposal on the ballot: Proposition 44 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-44-clinic-funding/). Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West wants voters to change how community health clinics spend money and penalize those that violate the ballot initiative’s provisions. The union claims too many clinics spend money inappropriately on things like high executive salaries rather than patient care. Clinics say they already prioritize patients and the initiative could bankrupt many facilities. While public interest in the billionaire tax fight dwarfs all other ballot measures, Prop. 44 is also shaping up to be contentious. Here’s what to know about it. What would the proposition do? Prop. 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) would require community health clinics, known as federally qualified health centers, to spend 90% of their revenue on “program services” that advance their mission to provide charitable care to low-income and uninsured patients. The proposition would prohibit clinics from spending more than 10% of revenue on other things such as administrative expenses. It would also penalize clinics that don’t meet the new 90% spending threshold. The attorney general could fine clinics that don’t comply, and the money would go into a special fund reserved for health workforce spending. Community health clinics are nonprofits that are required by law to reinvest 100% of revenue back into the organization regardless of how voters decide on Prop. 44. Most clinics spend about 80% of revenue providing health services, although some spend less, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026). Just one in three likely voters support the initiative, according to a September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). Who supports it? SEIU-UHW is the primary proponent of the initiative and has raised about $17 million to support the campaign, mainly from union coffers. The union tried last year to get lawmakers to pass a bill to do nearly the same thing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1113), but it died in committee. The group argues that dramatic federal healthcare cuts targeting programs for low-income patients make it crucial for clinics to spend money on patient services rather than administrative or other costs. “We’re seeing clinics that have extravagant fundraisers or art collections or CEOs that are paid in the millions while their patients are struggling to get appointments, while the workers are dealing with broken equipment,” union spokesperson Renee Saldana said. Saldana said the initiative is meant to secure spending for patients and workers, not take money away from clinics. It would also allow clinics to earn penalty money back if they come into compliance. Who opposes it? Opponents include groups representing clinics, doctors and hospitals as well as the unlikely bedfellows of the California Democratic, Republican and Working Families parties. They’ve collectively raised about $37.6 million against the measure. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Francisco Silva, chief executive of the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics, called the initiative an “existential threat.” Clinic spending is already highly regulated, Silva said, and the measure would force clinics to cut services, cut staff or close. Most clinics would pay a collective $1.7 billion in penalties in the first year and nearly half of all clinics in the state could close, according to a study commissioned by the primary care association (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf). “In many communities, the community health center is the only source of care,” Silva said. “You’re going to be losing the basic safety net if you lose half of the community health centers.” Silva said that the initiative would prevent clinics from spending on things like patient navigators, translators and food pantries. It would also prevent clinics, he said, from investing in capital improvements like renovations and new buildings. The union disagrees and says the initiative allows the attorney general to decide what type of spending counts toward patient services. If the Legislature rejected this, why put it on the ballot? Special interest groups have used ballot initiatives — or the threat of them — to gain political leverage for decades, but perhaps no other group has done so more effectively or prolifically as SEIU-UHW (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/06/health-ballot-measures-deal-billionaires/). The union, which represents 120,000 healthcare workers, has successfully used ballot initiatives to secure deals in Sacramento. Its biggest achievement was a $25 per hour health worker minimum wage (https://calmatters.org/health/2023/09/california-minimum-wage-health-care-workers/) in 2023. But the primary care association alleges those practices violate anti-racketeering laws (https://www.legalnewsline.com/northern-california-record/union-uses-ca-ballot-initiatives-to-strongarm-clinics-lawsuit/article_7c623996-6763-48fc-88bf-65d50af60749.html). In a complaint filed in September in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, the association and several clinics allege the union has unlawfully offered to kill Prop. 44 in exchange for more union membership at clinics or for the association to withdraw its opposition to the SEIU-UHW supported billionaire wealth tax. “Dave Regan and SEIU-UHW are extorting health centers by using the ballot measure process as as a way to get (the association) and health centers to agree to their demands that are entirely unrelated to Prop. 44,” said Joey Cachuela, general counsel for the primary care association, referencing the union’s president. Saldana said the allegations are “categorically false.” “This is the second time the (the association) has attempted to use legal filings to bully the healthcare workers of SEIU-UHW into backing down from holding clinics and CEOs accountable to patients,” she said. A judge dismissed a previous lawsuit filed by the primary care association to keep the initiative off the ballot. **Evaluating polling accuracy**

I've done considerable logical research, but for a thorough analysis, I think it's important to conduct primary polling and consider historical endorsements. Poll results like those from Prop 8 in 2018, as well as recent ones in 2020 and 2022, could be relevant, even if not strictly necessary. I can't really trust any odd forecasts that might skew results, so it’s clearer to focus on primary data.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) .
